sections.heading: AI Photography Fundamentals
sections.body:
AI photography uses machine learning to generate or enhance product images. You don't need a camera, studio, or photography skills—just clear direction and quality product references.

What AI Can Do:

  • Generate lifestyle scenes around your product
  • Replace backgrounds with professional environments
  • Create consistent lighting across product lines
  • Produce multiple variations for A/B testing

What You Still Need:

  • Clear photos of your actual product
  • Understanding of your target customer
  • Vision for how you want products presented

sections.heading: Preparing Your Product Photos
sections.body:
AI works best with good input. Here's how to prepare product reference photos:

Lighting: Natural daylight near a window. Avoid harsh shadows or mixed lighting.

Background: Plain white or neutral background. A white poster board works perfectly.

Angles: Take front, side, and three-quarter views. More angles = better AI understanding.

Focus: Sharp focus on the product. Avoid blur or motion.

Resolution: Highest resolution your phone allows. More pixels = more detail.

sections.heading: Understanding Prompts
sections.body:
Prompts are text instructions that guide AI generation. Good prompts include:

Scene Description: Where is the product? (marble bathroom counter, wooden kitchen table)

Lighting: What kind of light? (soft morning light, warm golden hour, bright studio)

Style: What aesthetic? (minimal, luxury, cozy, modern)

Camera Angle: What viewpoint? (straight-on, overhead flat lay, slight angle)

Props: What else is in the scene? (coffee cup, plant, towel)

Start simple and add detail as you get comfortable.

sections.heading: Common Beginner Mistakes
sections.body:
Avoid these pitfalls when starting with AI photography:

Over-Prompting: Too many details can confuse the AI. Start with 3-5 key elements.

Unrealistic Expectations: AI is a tool, not magic. Some results need iteration.

Ignoring Context: Your product should make sense in the scene. A protein powder doesn't belong on a bathroom vanity.

Inconsistent Lighting: Match lighting to scene type. Bathroom = soft morning light, kitchen = warm ambient.

Skipping Review: Always check details like shadows, reflections, and product accuracy before using.

sections.heading: Building Your First Collection
sections.body:
Start with a focused set of images:

  1. Hero Shot: Your product in its ideal environment, best lighting, most flattering angle.
  2. Clean Product Shot: Simple white background for listings and catalogs.
  3. In-Use Shot: Show the product being used (hands holding, pouring, applying).
  4. Detail Shot: Close-up on texture, label, or unique feature.
  5. Lifestyle Context: Product as part of a larger scene or routine.

These five shots cover most e-commerce needs.

sections.heading: Next Steps
sections.body:
Once you're comfortable with basics, explore advanced techniques:

Batch Generation: Create multiple variations to test performance.

Style Matching: Develop a consistent visual language across products.

Seasonal Updates: Refresh imagery for holidays, seasons, campaigns.

A/B Testing: Compare different scenes and styles to find what converts best.

Video Stills: Generate images designed to work as video thumbnails or stills.

The best way to learn is to experiment. Generate, review, iterate, and refine your approach.
